672	                                               Computational models are more likely to be implemented in applied sports settings if their
673	                                           accuracy, interpretability and functionality fit with the operation framework of a sports organ-
674	                                           isation[61]. In this case, BN provides an intuitive visualisation of the complex relationship of
675	                                           injuries, which medical staff may understand even with little or no experience in computer
676	                                           analytics. This may increase the model’s transparency and may improve the medical staff ’s
677	                                           trust in the model[62]. In terms of practical applicability, medical staff can use the model to
678	                                           create scenarios that facilitate the evaluation of different management options or the devel-
679	                                           opment of rehabilitation protocols for players with various positions or injuries occurring
680	                                           at different times during the season. These scenarios enable the assessment of the combined
681	                                           effects of risk factors[26]. This may enable them to proactively manage injury risk, and in case
682	                                           of injury, make more accurate predictions regarding the days to RTS for individual athletes
683	                                           based on epidemiological evidence. The BN can be modified to suit the specific context as
684	                                           determined by the user and updated with new information when available. In summary, BNs
685	                                           seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables in a complex system and may be
686	                                           further explored to support clinical decision making.
687	                                               The epidemiological data we used in this study is static; thus, we use a BN to represent the
688	                                           system as a time-aggregated model. However, most systems, including athletes, have been well
689	                                           recognised to change over time[4,63]. To capture the change over time and the feedback loops,
690	                                           a BN can be further extended into a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN)[64]. The DBN is an
691	                                           extension of the BNs and replicates the BN model at discrete points in time (time slices) and
692	                                           captures temporal relationships between the variables. DBNs can represent complex ques-
693	                                           tions, such as how changes in rehabilitation training load affect the time to RTS in athletes
694	                                           with different demographic and anthropometric characteristics. Modifiable variables, such
695	                                           as rehabilitation training exposure, can be collected continuously over time as time-series
696	                                           data[65]. DBNs have been applied in injury prediction[66], medical diagnosis or prognosis
697	                                           [67–69] and are also a promising avenue for further investigation in subsequent injury risk
698	                                           modelling. Specifically, DBNs may provide medical practitioners with a tool to predict the
699	                                           probability of a subsequent injury to occur given time-series data, such as injury history,
700	                                           recovery time and players’ physiological state over time. Future work could investigate using
701	                                           Wu et al. (2019)’s approach to analyse scenario-based complex systems[70].
702	
703	                                           Limitations
704	                                           The proposed BN model has limitations that should be considered when interpreting its results.
705	                                           Firstly, it is important to recognise that the model was constructed using data solely from the
706	                                           Bundesliga, and therefore, the generalisability of the results to other leagues or levels of play is
707	                                           limited. Second, the quality of the input variables directly impacts the model’s predictive accu-
708	                                           racy. In the case of our BN, it was constructed using basic epidemiological data sourced from
709	                                           public databases. While this approach maximises the availability of injury events for the model,
710	                                           it lacks pertinent information related to prognosis, such as diagnosis (e.g., structural damage or
711	                                           functional disorder) and the precise location of the injury (e.g., involvement of central tendon
712	                                           in hamstring injury) [71]. An accurate diagnosis of an injury plays a vital role in determining
713	                                           prognosis[10,72]. For instance, the recovery time to RTS can vary significantly between a minor
714	                                           partial tear in the hamstring muscle (requiring 17 days to RTS) and a moderate partial tear
715	                                           (requiring a longer time of 36 days to RTS). Therefore, the lack of detailed diagnostic informa-
716	                                           tion can impact the model’s graphical structure and prediction accuracy.
717	                                               Further studies may consider including more information into the model, such as quality
718	                                           and duration of rehabilitation training, RTS performance, reinjury incidence, the importance
719	                                           of upcoming competition, the remaining contract length, the club’s geographical regions
720	                                           and the players’ transfer value. Potentially, depending on the purpose of the model, we can

731	                                              Comparing the machine-learned BN with the existing scientific understanding of injury
732	                                           and recovery would also be a valuable future avenue of research. This comparison can provide

734	                                           a wide range of variables in contrast to a simpler model, such as an epidemiological one. By
735	                                           doing so, researchers can evaluate the added value of BN as a decision-support tool.

737	                                           Conclusion
738	                                           This discrete BN provides a decision support tool to help medical staff, coaches and players
739	                                           manage injury. The BN has a high sensitivity, ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 in predicting severity
740	                                           and provides a graphical representation of the investigated interdependencies. Medical staff
741	                                           can use BN to understand the strength of influence of different variables on the outcome and
742	                                           analyse the outcome based on custom RTS scenarios. This information may help medical staff
743	                                           evaluate different injury scenarios and better respond to individual player’s rehabilitation and
744	                                           team planning. BNs seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables from multiple
745	                                           sources and can be further explored to support clinical decision making.

                                           assessment, may be used to support coaches and players in predicting days to RTS and support
                                           team planning by assessing the number of players available for training and competition.
                                               In Fig 4, the thickness of the arcs indicates the strength of influence. Medical staff can use
                                           the strength of influence analysis to understand the local relationships among the variables
                                           in a network and how they contribute to the posterior marginal probability (i.e., outcome)
                                           for each node in the network (Fig 4). The strength of influence calculates the average effect
                                           of changing the state of a parent node on the probability distribution of states in the child
                                           node[60]. The arcs are normalised, thus the thickest arc indicates the one with the highest
                                           influence. From Fig 4, the nature of the injury (contact or non-contact) is related to the injury
                                           type and the body region. Injury type and body region are directly associated with the days_
                                           rts. Medical staff may use days_rts in conjunction with the clinical knowledge to project the
                                           rehabilitation timeline.

                                           Practical application and future developments
                                           The software we used for constructing the BN, GeNIe 2.0, could be used as a decision sup-
                                           port tool by sports practitioners, including but not limited to coaches, team managers, sports
                                           science and medical staff. Once the BN has been constructed, for example, with the use of
                                           GeNIe 2.0, the end users do not need any machine-learning knowledge or advanced computer
                                           skills to use the BN. Instead, the only input from the sports practitioners is to collect and
                                           input the players’ characteristics into the BN. The new data from every week or season can be
                                           input into the system’s database by data scientists (either in-house or third party) to ensure
                                           the model is up-to-date. As technology continues to advance, the process of constructing and
                                           utilising BN is expected to become easier and more efficient. This increased ease of use may
                                           encourage medical staff to invest their efforts in learning and adopting BNs to support their
                                           decision-making processes.
                                               When planning for RTS for an athlete, the BN can provide a personalised risk analysis
                                           from broad epidemiological data, as exemplified in section “Illustrative application of the BN”.
                                           While the results of the BN for estimating time to RTS align with existing clinical systems and
                                           therefore some practitioners may question the need for a computational decision support tool,
                                           it is important to see the potential benefits of integrating BN into sports medical practice in
                                           future. Conventional clinical guidelines often apply universally to all individuals regardless of
                                           age, sex, sport, or level of play. Consequently, they are not intended to offer an individualised
                                           approach to RTS estimation. Given that athletes’ diverse needs and circumstances, coupled
                                           with the growing emphasis on personalised and precision medicine, a more tailored approach
                                           to estimating RTS becomes essential. In this regard, the incorporation of BN can serve as a
                                           valuable addition to sports medical practice to improve decision making.
                                               In our example, we explained the use of BN with a RTS scenario and estimated the time to
                                           RTS based on a player’s basic characteristics. However, it is important to note that this study
                                           is a pilot for future studies, and the potential applications of BN extend beyond this specific
                                           use case. They can be leveraged for various purposes, such as forecasting expected perfor-
                                           mance or injury risk in a game by considering factors like personal characteristics, opponent
                                           playing style, and recent training and game performance. While in this study, the BN yielded
                                           similar results to existing clinical systems, its true benefits lie in its ease of use, efficiency, and
                                           the capacity to incorporate a wider range of data into the decision-making process. The BN’s
                                           ability to identify the strength of influence allows medical staff to address the variables that
                                           significantly impact outcomes, a task that cannot be adequately addressed by conventional
                                           clinical guidelines alone. By leveraging BN, medical staff may enhance their decision-making
                                           processes and provide more tailored and effective care to athletes.



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0314184 March 20, 2025                                                                        13 / 19
 PLOS ONE                                                                               Using a Bayesian network to classify time to return to sport



                                               Computational models are more likely to be implemented in applied sports settings if their
                                           accuracy, interpretability and functionality fit with the operation framework of a sports organ-
                                           isation[61]. In this case, BN provides an intuitive visualisation of the complex relationship of
                                           injuries, which medical staff may understand even with little or no experience in computer
                                           analytics. This may increase the model’s transparency and may improve the medical staff ’s
                                           trust in the model[62]. In terms of practical applicability, medical staff can use the model to
                                           create scenarios that facilitate the evaluation of different management options or the devel-
                                           opment of rehabilitation protocols for players with various positions or injuries occurring
                                           at different times during the season. These scenarios enable the assessment of the combined
                                           effects of risk factors[26]. This may enable them to proactively manage injury risk, and in case
                                           of injury, make more accurate predictions regarding the days to RTS for individual athletes
                                           based on epidemiological evidence. The BN can be modified to suit the specific context as
                                           determined by the user and updated with new information when available. In summary, BNs
                                           seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables in a complex system and may be
                                           further explored to support clinical decision making.
                                               The epidemiological data we used in this study is static; thus, we use a BN to represent the
                                           system as a time-aggregated model. However, most systems, including athletes, have been well
                                           recognised to change over time[4,63]. To capture the change over time and the feedback loops,
                                           a BN can be further extended into a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN)[64]. The DBN is an
                                           extension of the BNs and replicates the BN model at discrete points in time (time slices) and
                                           captures temporal relationships between the variables. DBNs can represent complex ques-
                                           tions, such as how changes in rehabilitation training load affect the time to RTS in athletes
                                           with different demographic and anthropometric characteristics. Modifiable variables, such
                                           as rehabilitation training exposure, can be collected continuously over time as time-series
                                           data[65]. DBNs have been applied in injury prediction[66], medical diagnosis or prognosis
                                           [67–69] and are also a promising avenue for further investigation in subsequent injury risk
                                           modelling. Specifically, DBNs may provide medical practitioners with a tool to predict the
                                           probability of a subsequent injury to occur given time-series data, such as injury history,
                                           recovery time and players’ physiological state over time. Future work could investigate using
                                           Wu et al. (2019)’s approach to analyse scenario-based complex systems[70].

                                           Limitations
                                           The proposed BN model has limitations that should be considered when interpreting its results.
                                           Firstly, it is important to recognise that the model was constructed using data solely from the
                                           Bundesliga, and therefore, the generalisability of the results to other leagues or levels of play is
                                           limited. Second, the quality of the input variables directly impacts the model’s predictive accu-
                                           racy. In the case of our BN, it was constructed using basic epidemiological data sourced from
                                           public databases. While this approach maximises the availability of injury events for the model,
                                           it lacks pertinent information related to prognosis, such as diagnosis (e.g., structural damage or
                                           functional disorder) and the precise location of the injury (e.g., involvement of central tendon
                                           in hamstring injury) [71]. An accurate diagnosis of an injury plays a vital role in determining
                                           prognosis[10,72]. For instance, the recovery time to RTS can vary significantly between a minor
                                           partial tear in the hamstring muscle (requiring 17 days to RTS) and a moderate partial tear
                                           (requiring a longer time of 36 days to RTS). Therefore, the lack of detailed diagnostic informa-
                                           tion can impact the model’s graphical structure and prediction accuracy.
                                               Further studies may consider including more information into the model, such as quality
                                           and duration of rehabilitation training, RTS performance, reinjury incidence, the importance
                                           of upcoming competition, the remaining contract length, the club’s geographical regions
                                           and the players’ transfer value. Potentially, depending on the purpose of the model, we can

                                           integrate epidemiological data from other larger datasets into the model to enlarge the data-
                                           base to reduce the chance of overfitting and improve result transportability.
                                              Comparing the machine-learned BN with the existing scientific understanding of injury
                                           and recovery would also be a valuable future avenue of research. This comparison can provide
                                           insights into the performance and predictive capabilities of a complex model that incorporates
                                           a wide range of variables in contrast to a simpler model, such as an epidemiological one. By
                                           doing so, researchers can evaluate the added value of BN as a decision-support tool.

                                           Conclusion
                                           This discrete BN provides a decision support tool to help medical staff, coaches and players
                                           manage injury. The BN has a high sensitivity, ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 in predicting severity
                                           and provides a graphical representation of the investigated interdependencies. Medical staff
                                           can use BN to understand the strength of influence of different variables on the outcome and
                                           analyse the outcome based on custom RTS scenarios. This information may help medical staff
                                           evaluate different injury scenarios and better respond to individual player’s rehabilitation and
                                           team planning. BNs seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables from multiple
                                           sources and can be further explored to support clinical decision making.

33	                                                               Abstract:
34	                                                               This study aimed to investigate the recovery of neuromuscular performance using mechanical parameters collected during
35	                                                               jump (vertical and horizontal) and strength-power exercises in youth soccer players after official soccer matches. Twenty-one
36	                                                               outfield highly trained youth male soccer athletes (age: 18.23 ± 0.73 years; weight: 72.12 ± 6.99 kg; height: 1.78 ± 0.08 m)
37	                                                               from two teams competing in the 1st division of U-19 Portuguese National Championship participated in this study. Players
38	                                                               completed a battery of physical tests at -2h, +30 min, +24h, and +48h in relation to the match. Countermovement jump height,
39	                                                               horizontal jump distance, and bar velocity during the half-squat, bench press, and hip-thrust exercises, at fixed loads, were
40	                                                               recorded. Countermovement jump was impaired until 24h post-match (-1.7% from pre to 24h post, p=0.050; ES=-0.82). Half-
41	                                                               squat bar velocity was reduced immediately following the match (-6.8 % from pre- p=0.004; ES=-0.64) but recovered at +24h
42	                                                               (+2.9%, p=1.00; ES=0.02). Hip-thrust bar velocity was reduced for up to 48h post-match (-7.4% from pre to 48h post, p<0.001;
43	                                                               ES=-0.80). No impairments were found in the horizontal jump and bench press at any moment. Our findings show prolonged
44	                                                               decrements in strength of the posterior chain following a soccer match, measured in the hip-thrust exercise, while the other
45	                                                               exercises displayed faster recovery dynamics.

                                                               jump (vertical and horizontal) and strength-power exercises in youth soccer players after official soccer matches. Twenty-one
                                                               outfield highly trained youth male soccer athletes (age: 18.23 ± 0.73 years; weight: 72.12 ± 6.99 kg; height: 1.78 ± 0.08 m)
                                                               from two teams competing in the 1st division of U-19 Portuguese National Championship participated in this study. Players
                                                               completed a battery of physical tests at -2h, +30 min, +24h, and +48h in relation to the match. Countermovement jump height,

                                                               squat bar velocity was reduced immediately following the match (-6.8 % from pre- p=0.004; ES=-0.64) but recovered at +24h
                                                               (+2.9%, p=1.00; ES=0.02). Hip-thrust bar velocity was reduced for up to 48h post-match (-7.4% from pre to 48h post, p<0.001;
                                                               ES=-0.80). No impairments were found in the horizontal jump and bench press at any moment. Our findings show prolonged
                                                               decrements in strength of the posterior chain following a soccer match, measured in the hip-thrust exercise, while the other

                                                               25   Soccer players deal with very-high physical demands during matches that are related to

                                                               26   acute and delayed manifestations of fatigue [1,2]. In fact, high-intensity activities are

                                                               27   progressively reduced toward the end of the second half of the match [3,4] and physical

                                                               28   performance is impaired immediately after competitive soccer matches [1,5]. This

                                                               29   decrement in physical performance and increased signs of muscle damage and

                                                               31   research has been conducted to better understand match-induced neuromuscular fatigue

                                                               32   [4], the knowledge about the time required to fully recover the neuromuscular

                                                               33   performance in different exercises following official matches in youth soccer players is




                                                                                                                                                                  Accepted Manuscript
                                                               34   limited [2,6]. This is particularly relevant for professionals planning recovery strategies

                                                               35   and implementing strength and conditioning practices.


                                                               36   Despite the recognized importance of resistance training during the in-season period for

                                                               37   soccer players [7,8], the optimal timing of the sessions within the weekly training

                                                               38   schedule remains debatable [9]. For example, to minimize post-match fatigue effects,

                                                               39   strength-power training sessions are usually prescribed 72h following the match day

                                                               40   (MD+3 to MD-2). However, previous studies have shown that performing resistance

                                                               41   training at 24h and 48h post-match (MD+1 and MD+2) did not compromise the

                                                               42   recovery kinetics from the match and the quality of resistance training sessions (e.g., the

                                                               43   force produced) [9,10]. Therefore, understanding the kinetics of neuromuscular

                                                               44   recovery under different muscle contraction conditions (e.g., using or not using the

                                                               45   stretch-shortening cycle) following soccer matches may be relevant for practitioners in

                                                               46   scheduling training practices based on players’ readiness to train. Moreover, it is

                                                               47   important to examine whether a similar time course of recovery (i.e., 48-72h post-match
                                                                48   for semi-professional soccer players) [1,11] applies to younger players, since fitter

                                                               49   athletes tend to experience lower metabolic disturbances, muscle damage, and acute

                                                               50   fatigue following a match [12].


                                                               51   Irrespective of the mechanisms underpinning neuromuscular decrements, match-play

                                                               52   fatigue response can be quantified using valid functional tests (e.g., jump performance)

                                                               53   related to soccer performance or considered to reflect neuromuscular function [13].




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               54   While vertical jumps (countermovement jump [CMJ], squat jump, drop jump) are valid,

                                                               55   reliable, and commonly used for detecting match-related fatigue [5,14], there is limited

                                                               56   information regarding the usefulness of bar velocity against submaximal resistances




                                                                                                                                                                            Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               57   [15] for the same purpose. While assessing neuromuscular fatigue using jumping




                                                                                                                                                               Accepted Manuscript
                                                               58   exercises implies additional testing and time requirements for the staff and players,

                                                               59   using bar velocity would represent less time spent assessing the players as it can be

                                                               60   performed during their usual resistance training, and not as a separate test. Scientific

                                                               61   evidence suggests that reduction in bar velocity can reflect neuromuscular impairment,

                                                               62   due to its strong relationship with markers of metabolic disturbance and post-training

                                                               63   decrements in muscle strength [15]. Recently, Callaghan et al. (2022) [16] reported

                                                               64   significant decrements in measures of back squat movement velocity up to 48h post-

                                                               65   match, as well as a decrease in CMJ height at 24h post-match in sub-elite male rugby

                                                               66   players. However, different team-sport disciplines (i.e., rugby league vs. soccer) have

                                                               67   different physical and physiological demands, which certainly influence acute and

                                                               68   delayed fatigue responses following matches [17]. Thus, it seems relevant to analyze

                                                               69   and quantify the post-match fatigue using the bar velocity approach in high-level soccer

                                                               70   players.
                                                                71   In practical terms, the velocity-based training (VBT) approach can be used to assess

                                                               72   movement velocity in different exercises (e.g., squat and bench press) and estimate

                                                               73   neuromuscular fatigue during resistance training sessions (i.e., half-squat, hip-thrust,

                                                               74   and bench press), with minimal interruption to training routine [16]. This is important

                                                               75   because different muscle groups may present distinct post-effort fatigue and recovery

                                                               76   profiles that could affect the players’ readiness to train. For example, hamstrings muscle

                                                               77   strength was moderate to largely reduced up to 72h post-match, which is long-lasting in




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               78   comparison to quadriceps (trivial reduction at 48h) [2]. Accordingly, the hip-thrust

                                                               79   exercise may reflect muscle damage and fatigue in hamstrings and gluteus maximus due

                                                               80   to the high eccentric strain imposed upon these muscles during sprints and directional

                                                               81   changes [2,18,19]. However, to the best of our knowledge, no studies have examined

                                                               82   the hip-thrust bar velocity in the days following soccer matches.


                                                               83   It is important to highlight that these exercises (i.e., CMJ, half-squat, hip-thrust) are

                                                               84   usually prescribed throughout the season to improve power, speed, and jumping ability

                                                               85   and to reduce the risk of injury in soccer players. Hence, examining the time-course of

                                                               86   recovery of the aforementioned exercises following a soccer match could help

                                                               87   practitioners define which exercises and training modes (e.g., plyometrics) could be

                                                               88   used at MD+1 and MD+2 to develop strength-power qualities of soccer players,

                                                               89   avoiding the undesired pre-training fatigue that can impair training quality and

                                                               90   adaptation [10,20]. Furthermore, upper-body resistance training may be used in soccer

                                                               91   as an active form of post-match recovery, purportedly activating some physiological

                                                               92   mechanisms (i.e., increased blood flow and hormonal responses) without involving

                                                               93   (pre) damaged or fatigued muscle groups [10]. In addition, this also helps players

                                                               94   optimize the development of some soccer-specific physical capacities such as sprinting

                                                               95   due to the contribution of arms during sprinting tasks [21].
                                                                 96   Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the recovery of neuromuscular performance

                                                                97   using mechanical parameters collected during jump (vertical and horizontal) and

                                                                98   strength-power exercises in youth soccer players after official soccer matches. We

                                                                99   hypothesized that all assessments would reflect immediate and delayed (24h and 48h

                                                               100   post-match) impairments in neuromuscular function and that performance in gluteus

                                                               101   maximus- and hamstrings-dominant exercises (i.e., hip-thrust and horizontal jump) [19]

                                                               102   would take longer to recover. This knowledge might help define the appropriate

                                                               103   moments to prescribe plyometrics and the resistance exercises within a competitive

                                                               104   microcycle.

                                                               107   A cross-sectional design was used to examine the acute and delayed effects of official

                                                               112   half-squat, bench press, and hip-thrust exercises. Prior to the match day (MD), the

                                                               113   soccer players were required to attend 3 testing sessions across 3 different days (MD-4,

                                                               114   MD-3, and MD-2) at their respective training facilities (Figure 1) to determine the

                                                                120   horizontal jump metrics were measured up to 48h after the match (post-match +30 min;

                                                               121   + 24h [MD+1]; and +48h [MD+2]), in which the official match (0h [MD]) at home

200	140 19 Portuguese National Championship (highest national division for the specific age
201	141 group), with at least 1 year of strength training experience including all exercises used
202	142 in the current study, were recruited to participate in this study. Players who were on the
203	143 field for less than 30 min were excluded from the analysis. Thus, a total of 21 soccer
204	144 players (age: 18.42 ± 0.74 years; weight: 72.49 ± 6.97 kg; height: 1.78 ± 0.07 m) who
205	145 played a minimum of 60 min during one game were included in the study. The study
206	146 design was carefully explained to the participants, and written informed consents were
207	147 obtained from players and their legal guardians (<18 years) prior to data collection. The
208	148 study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee
209	149 of the University of Maia (63/2022).
210	150 Strength-power assessments
211	151 Strength-power assessments were performed throughout the microcycle prior to the
212	152 match (MD-4, MD-3, and MD-2), considering player availability. Prior to testing,
213	153 participants warmed-up by performing low-intensity cycling exercise (5 min), mobility
214	154 exercises (5 min), and submaximal sets of half-squats, bench press, and hip-thrust
215	155 exercises (1 x 5 repetitions at 20 kg (i.e., unloaded barbell) (Figure 1). Thereafter, a
216	156 progressive loading test up to ~80% of e1RM was performed for each exercise to fit an
217	157 individual load-velocity relationship. Players were given the necessary passive rest time
218	158 (3-5 min) before performing a new lift to ensure full recovery. This submaximal method
219	159 was selected to avoid unnecessary risks and fatigue of lifting heavier loads [22].
220	160 Descriptive data of the loads and mean propulsive velocities (MPVs) used in this study
221	161 for each resistance exercise are displayed in Table 1. The MPV is calculated from the
222	162 portion of the concentric phase in which the measured acceleration [α] is greater than
223	163 the acceleration due to gravity (α > -9.81 m∙s-2) [23]. The technique used for each
224	164 resistance exercise included in our study was previously detailed elsewhere [24–26].
225	165 The initial testing load for each exercise was set as: 40 kg for the half-squat and bench
226	166 press, and 60 kg for the hip-thrust. The load was gradually increased by 20 kg, and then
227	167 10 kg, when a MPV of 0.75 – 0.90 m∙s-1 was attained, in the half-squat and hip-thrust,
228	168 and by increments of 10 kg in the bench press, until a velocity related to ~80% of e1RM
229	169 was reached. Participants received real-time feedback on the MPV and verbal
230	170 encouragement to exert their maximum effort during the concentric phase of the
231	171 movement. The eccentric phase of the lift was performed in a continuous and controlled
232	172 manner (0.50 to 0.65 m∙s-1) with a momentary pause between the eccentric and
233	173 concentric portion of the lifting (~1.5 s) to provide more reliable data [27].
234	174 To assess the pre- to post-match change in bar velocity, players completed two
235	repetitions for each resistance exercise at ~70% of the e1RM. This range of loads was
236	175
237	176 adjusted by approximation, as presented in Table 1, with athletes being grouped by
238	177 strength level. That is, athletes with similar loads (within ~5 kg) for the defined
239	178 percentage of 1-RM (~70% of e1RM) performed the exercise with the same weight.
240	179 Displacement and MPV of the bar were recorded during each repetition for the half-
241	180 squat, hip-thrust, and bench press exercises using a linear encoder (Vitruve, Madrid,
242	181 Spain) [28,29]. The Vitruve (previously, Speed4Lift) measures the cable displacement
243	182 in response to a change in the bar position during the lift at a sampling frequency of 100
244	183 Hz.
245	184 Vertical and horizontal jump tests

323	262 DISCUSSION
324	263 We investigated the recovery of neuromuscular performance using metrics recorded
325	264 during jump and strength-power tests in youth soccer players after official matches. The
326	265 CMJh was impaired for up to 24h post-match (-1.7% at post 24h; p = 0.050; ES = -0.82).
327	266 Performance in the hip-thrust decreased immediately after the match (-12.3%; p <
328	267 0.001; ES = -0.88) and remained reduced at 48h post-match (-7.4%; p < 0.001; ES = -
329	268 0.80). Contrary to what was hypothesized [16], decreases in half-squat bar velocity were
330	269 only significant following the match (-6.8% from pre- to post-match, ; p = 0.004; ES = -
331	270 0.64), returning to baseline after 24h (+2.9%, p=1.00; ES=0.02). Additionally, no
332	271 significant differences were observed in the HJ d and bench press bar velocity from pre-
333	272 to post-match time points, except for an improved HJd at 48h post-match. Due to the
334	273 high loading of the posterior chain during soccer matches, it was hypothesized that
335	274 movements primarily recruiting the gluteus maximus and hamstrings would take longer
336	275 time to recover. This was partially confirmed by our data showing that reductions in the
337	276 hip-thrust bar velocity persisted for 48h after the match.
338	277 In line with previous studies [2,5,18], soccer matches resulted in impaired
339	278 neuromuscular performance that persisted for 24-48h post-match. CMJh in the current
340	279 study declined post-match (6.79%) and at 24h but recovered just after 48h. These results
341	280 diverge from existing evidence at the post-48h time point. For instance, de Hoyo et al.
342	281 [5] reported a peak decrease in CMJh after 24h, but performance remained impaired at
343	282 48h post-match. Similarly, Nedelec et al. [18] showed an ~7.5% decrease in jump
344	283 height 48h after a match in senior professional soccer players. Finally, Magalhães et al.
345	284 [33] reported an ~12% CMJh decrease at 48h. Several studies did not observe any
346	285 meaningful changes in CMJh following competition or intermittent exercise [14,34].
347	286 Thus, it could be argued that CMJh alone may not be sensitive enough to measure acute
348	287 or residual neuromuscular fatigue [14,34], at least in conditions of relatively low
349	288 fatigue, as was probably the case at +48h post-match. Furthermore, there is a possibility
350	289 that athletes can maintain jump height even under the presence of fatigue by increasing
351	290 the length of the CMJ eccentric phase or the CMJ total contraction time [5]. Thus, there
352	291 seems to exist substantial variability in the CMJ h decreases following real or simulated
353	292 soccer matches or other high-intensity and intermittent sports. Additionally, it is
354	293 important to consider that Nedelec et al. [18] analyzed professional senior soccer
355	294 players and Magalhães et al. [33] investigated senior professional and semi-professional
356	295 soccer players. Nonetheless, our results agree with those reported by Brownstein et al.
357	296 [1] showing that CMJh decreased immediately post- and 24h after a match, but returned
358	297 to baseline values at 48h, aligning with measures of central and peripheral fatigue.
359	298 Regarding the half-squat, a 5.05% decrease in MPV was noted, but performance was
360	299 recovered after just 24h. Callaghan et al. [16] have used a similar approach in rugby
361	300 players. The authors found significant decrements in the back squat mean velocity at 30
362	301 min, 24h, and 48h post-match. However, there are methodological differences between
363	302 the studies. The authors of that study used a different and lighter load, corresponding to
364	303 a mean velocity of 1m.s-1 (V1load). In our study, the “baseline” (pre-match) MPV was
365	304 slower (0.69 ± 0.1 m.s-1), which means that the load lifted was relatively heavier,
366	305 corresponding to ~70% of the e1RM. Additionally, the aforementioned authors
367	306 hypothesized that the greater range of motion and stretch on the impaired musculature
368	307 resulting from the squat (femurs approximately parallel to the floor during the eccentric
369	308 portion of the exercise) may have contributed to the detection of neuromuscular fatigue.
370	309 Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that, compared to soccer, rugby is likely more
371	310 physically demanding in terms of physical contact. In addition, heavy rugby players
372	311 apply very high eccentric forces during decelerations due to their sprint momentum
373	312 [35]. Short high-intensity actions such as accelerations/decelerations, and sprinting are
374	313 commonly observed in soccer matches and have been associated with muscle damage,
375	314 thus affecting subsequent recovery kinetics [18,36]. Decreases in maximum voluntary
376	315 contraction torque associated with muscle damage have been extensively studied [6,11]
377	316 and seem to be a consequence of impairments in contractile function and/or the capacity
378	317 of the central nervous system to effectively activate the muscle [1]. It seems that muscle
379	318 damage and fatigue are attenuated in less than 24h for the half-squat exercise in young
380	319 soccer players, allowing them to use this exercise early in the competitive schedule
381	320 (e.g., MD+1).
382	321 In contrast with the time course of the half-squat, performance in the hip-thrust exercise
383	322 was impaired from post-match up to 48h. Greater impairments in the hamstring muscles
384	323 compared to the quadriceps have been shown to prevail up to 72h post-match [2].
385	324 Accordingly, decrements in neuromuscular performance and increases in muscle
386	325 soreness of the hamstrings have been previously reported following soccer-simulated
387	326 intermittent running exercises and other team sports’ matches with high eccentric
388	327 components [37,38]. An increase in soccer training-related hamstring injury rates has
389	328 been reported, in comparison to competition-related injuries [39], and this might be
390	329 related to the increased match demands and/or players experiencing high training loads
391	330 during recovery periods [2]. Furthermore, given that gluteus maximum is highly taxed
392	331 during soccer specific actions (e.g., sprint) [40], prolonged post-match fatigue/damage
393	332 in this muscle likely help explain the recovery kinetics of hip-thrust, an exercise that
394	333 highly activates the gluteus [41]. Since muscle damage and fatigue in the hip-thrust
395	334 persists for at least 48h following the match, exercises/movements that place more
396	335 mechanical stress on the gluteus and hamstring muscles should be avoided at MD+1 and
397	336 MD+2.
398	337 On the other hand, bar velocity in the bench press exercise remained constant
399	338 throughout the post-match period. Thus, upper body resistance training (at least pushing
400	339 exercises such as the bench press) on the days following a match might be feasible.
401	340 Scheduling upper body resistance training might help preserving upper body strength
402	341 [10]. Since upper-body resistance training seems to fit in the first sessions post-match,
403	342 exercises such as bench press can be easily implemented in the competitive microcycle,
404	343 especially due to the role of upper body in actions such as sprinting and body contacts
405	344 [21].
406	345 Lastly, HJ performance did not decrease across the observed period and even an
407	346 increase in HJ distance was observed at 48h post-match. The hip-thrust and HJ exercises
408	347 share some similarities, with both movements being performed using the anteroposterior
409	348 force-vector [42]. Thus, it was initially hypothesized that both exercises would follow
410	349 similar recovery kinetics after the match. However, it is worth mentioning that force
411	350 application differs substantially between them, since the HJ is a very fast horizontally
412	351 oriented movement performed without external loading. In contrast, the hip-thrust was
413	352 executed at a moderate-to-high loading condition (~70% of e1RM). Furthermore, even
414	353 though players were instructed to maintain a similar jumping technique during all
415	354 assessments, a change in technique to accommodate the resultant fatigue is a possibility.
416	355 Similarly, familiarization to the HJ during testing sessions cannot be ruled out;
417	356 however, all players performed HJs regularly in their clubs. According to our results,
418	357 unloaded HJs may be performed on the day following the match or even combined with
419	358 CMJs 48h post-match (MD+2/-4).
420	359
421	360 LIMITATIONS
422	361 Our study has some limitations. First, because the study was conducted during the
423	competitive season, using the traditional approach to determine the 1RM load was not
424	362
425	363 possible. Therefore, a submaximal load was selected to avoid unnecessary risks and
426	364 fatigue when lifting heavier loads [22]. A larger sample size with a longer follow-up
427	365 period (more athletes and more matches) could allow different sub-analyzes (i.e.,
428	366 starters vs. non-starters, stronger vs. weaker athletes) across multiple time-points. The
429	367 order of the exercises performed was not randomized, and this could also be considered
430	368 a limitation. Lastly, only the external match loads were monitored, without considering
431	369 training loads and well-being status throughout the week.
432	370
433	371 CONCLUSION
434	372 In conclusion, the posterior chain strength as measured by the hip-thrust exercise takes
435	373 more than 48h to recover after a match. This means that prescribing such exercise
436	374 during strength-power training sessions deserves caution on MD+1 and MD+2. Other
437	375 loaded exercises, such as the half-squat, is fully recovered after the 24h post-match,
438	376 while performance in the bench press is not affected by the match. Hence, these
439	377 exercises can be programmed in the first days interspersing two consecutive matches.
440	378 Finally, HJ performance is immediately recovered after the match, while CMJh takes
441	379 only 48h to return to baseline values. This finding indicates that plyometric exercises in
442	380 the post-match days can stress first the horizontal (MD+1) and later the vertical force
443	381 vector (MD+2 on) within a competitive youth soccer microcycle.

286 Thus, it could be argued that CMJh alone may not be sensitive enough to measure acute
287 or residual neuromuscular fatigue [14,34], at least in conditions of relatively low
288 fatigue, as was probably the case at +48h post-match. Furthermore, there is a possibility
289 that athletes can maintain jump height even under the presence of fatigue by increasing
290 the length of the CMJ eccentric phase or the CMJ total contraction time [5]. Thus, there
291 seems to exist substantial variability in the CMJ h decreases following real or simulated
292 soccer matches or other high-intensity and intermittent sports. Additionally, it is
293 important to consider that Nedelec et al. [18] analyzed professional senior soccer
294 players and Magalhães et al. [33] investigated senior professional and semi-professional
295 soccer players. Nonetheless, our results agree with those reported by Brownstein et al.
296 [1] showing that CMJh decreased immediately post- and 24h after a match, but returned
297 to baseline values at 48h, aligning with measures of central and peripheral fatigue.
298 Regarding the half-squat, a 5.05% decrease in MPV was noted, but performance was
299 recovered after just 24h. Callaghan et al. [16] have used a similar approach in rugby
300 players. The authors found significant decrements in the back squat mean velocity at 30
301 min, 24h, and 48h post-match. However, there are methodological differences between
302 the studies. The authors of that study used a different and lighter load, corresponding to
303 a mean velocity of 1m.s-1 (V1load). In our study, the “baseline” (pre-match) MPV was
304 slower (0.69 ± 0.1 m.s-1), which means that the load lifted was relatively heavier,
305 corresponding to ~70% of the e1RM. Additionally, the aforementioned authors
306 hypothesized that the greater range of motion and stretch on the impaired musculature
307 resulting from the squat (femurs approximately parallel to the floor during the eccentric
308 portion of the exercise) may have contributed to the detection of neuromuscular fatigue.
309 Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that, compared to soccer, rugby is likely more
310 physically demanding in terms of physical contact. In addition, heavy rugby players
311 apply very high eccentric forces during decelerations due to their sprint momentum
312 [35]. Short high-intensity actions such as accelerations/decelerations, and sprinting are
313 commonly observed in soccer matches and have been associated with muscle damage,
314 thus affecting subsequent recovery kinetics [18,36]. Decreases in maximum voluntary
315 contraction torque associated with muscle damage have been extensively studied [6,11]
316 and seem to be a consequence of impairments in contractile function and/or the capacity
317 of the central nervous system to effectively activate the muscle [1]. It seems that muscle
318 damage and fatigue are attenuated in less than 24h for the half-squat exercise in young
319 soccer players, allowing them to use this exercise early in the competitive schedule
320 (e.g., MD+1).
321 In contrast with the time course of the half-squat, performance in the hip-thrust exercise
322 was impaired from post-match up to 48h. Greater impairments in the hamstring muscles
323 compared to the quadriceps have been shown to prevail up to 72h post-match [2].
324 Accordingly, decrements in neuromuscular performance and increases in muscle
325 soreness of the hamstrings have been previously reported following soccer-simulated
326 intermittent running exercises and other team sports’ matches with high eccentric
327 components [37,38]. An increase in soccer training-related hamstring injury rates has
328 been reported, in comparison to competition-related injuries [39], and this might be
329 related to the increased match demands and/or players experiencing high training loads
330 during recovery periods [2]. Furthermore, given that gluteus maximum is highly taxed
331 during soccer specific actions (e.g., sprint) [40], prolonged post-match fatigue/damage
332 in this muscle likely help explain the recovery kinetics of hip-thrust, an exercise that
333 highly activates the gluteus [41]. Since muscle damage and fatigue in the hip-thrust
334 persists for at least 48h following the match, exercises/movements that place more
335 mechanical stress on the gluteus and hamstring muscles should be avoided at MD+1 and
336 MD+2.
337 On the other hand, bar velocity in the bench press exercise remained constant
338 throughout the post-match period. Thus, upper body resistance training (at least pushing
339 exercises such as the bench press) on the days following a match might be feasible.
340 Scheduling upper body resistance training might help preserving upper body strength
341 [10]. Since upper-body resistance training seems to fit in the first sessions post-match,
342 exercises such as bench press can be easily implemented in the competitive microcycle,
343 especially due to the role of upper body in actions such as sprinting and body contacts
344 [21].
345 Lastly, HJ performance did not decrease across the observed period and even an
346 increase in HJ distance was observed at 48h post-match. The hip-thrust and HJ exercises
347 share some similarities, with both movements being performed using the anteroposterior
348 force-vector [42]. Thus, it was initially hypothesized that both exercises would follow
349 similar recovery kinetics after the match. However, it is worth mentioning that force
350 application differs substantially between them, since the HJ is a very fast horizontally
351 oriented movement performed without external loading. In contrast, the hip-thrust was
352 executed at a moderate-to-high loading condition (~70% of e1RM). Furthermore, even
353 though players were instructed to maintain a similar jumping technique during all
354 assessments, a change in technique to accommodate the resultant fatigue is a possibility.
355 Similarly, familiarization to the HJ during testing sessions cannot be ruled out;
356 however, all players performed HJs regularly in their clubs. According to our results,
357 unloaded HJs may be performed on the day following the match or even combined with
358 CMJs 48h post-match (MD+2/-4).
359
360 LIMITATIONS
361 Our study has some limitations. First, because the study was conducted during the
competitive season, using the traditional approach to determine the 1RM load was not
362
363 possible. Therefore, a submaximal load was selected to avoid unnecessary risks and
364 fatigue when lifting heavier loads [22]. A larger sample size with a longer follow-up
365 period (more athletes and more matches) could allow different sub-analyzes (i.e.,
366 starters vs. non-starters, stronger vs. weaker athletes) across multiple time-points. The
367 order of the exercises performed was not randomized, and this could also be considered
368 a limitation. Lastly, only the external match loads were monitored, without considering
369 training loads and well-being status throughout the week.
370
371 CONCLUSION
372 In conclusion, the posterior chain strength as measured by the hip-thrust exercise takes
373 more than 48h to recover after a match. This means that prescribing such exercise
374 during strength-power training sessions deserves caution on MD+1 and MD+2. Other
375 loaded exercises, such as the half-squat, is fully recovered after the 24h post-match,
376 while performance in the bench press is not affected by the match. Hence, these
377 exercises can be programmed in the first days interspersing two consecutive matches.
378 Finally, HJ performance is immediately recovered after the match, while CMJh takes
379 only 48h to return to baseline values. This finding indicates that plyometric exercises in
380 the post-match days can stress first the horizontal (MD+1) and later the vertical force
381 vector (MD+2 on) within a competitive youth soccer microcycle.
382

391 Fatigue following Competitive Soccer Match-Play. Front Physiol 2017; 8.
392 doi:https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2017.00831

79	ABSTRACT
80	Objective: The primary aim of this study was to assess the efficacy of the weight, urine, thirst
81	(WUT) framework in predicting dehydration after a body water manipulation protocol, while
82	concurrently determining the individual and interactive contributions of the model components.
83	D
84	Methods: The total study sample was 93 participants (female, n = 47), recruited from two
85	institutions. Phase 1 involved collecting daily hydration measures from free-living participants
86	EP
87	(Study 1, 58 participants for 3 days; Study 2, 35 participants for 7 days). Phase 2 entailed a two-
88	hour passive heating protocol, where participants from Study 2 were randomly assigned to one of
89	TE
90	three groups that manipulated total body water over 24-hours using passive heating and fluid
91	restriction. During each Phase, participants provided urine samples, underwent body mass
92	measurements, and completed questionnaires pertaining to thirst perception. Morning and 24-
93	hour urine samples were assessed for color, osmolality, and specific gravity. Differences
94	between intervention groups, based on the probability of hydration status, were examined
95	C
96	(ANOVA) and ridge regression analysis assessed the relative importance of variables within the
97	C
98	WUT model.
99	A
100	Results: The study revealed significant differences among the intervention groups for predicted
101	probability of dehydration, as determined by changes in body mass (p = 0.001), urine color (p =
102	0.044), and thirst perception (p < 0.001). Binomial ridge regression indicated that change in body
103	mass (58%) and thirst perception (26%) were the most influential predictors of dehydration.
104	Conclusions: These data support use of an enhanced version of the WUT model, underscoring
105	the significance of changes in body mass and thirst perception in the assessment of hydration
106	status.
107	Key Words: WATER, URINE SPECIFIC GRAVITY, BODY MASS, FLUID INTAKE, BODY
108	WATER REGULATION, THIRST PERCEPTION

115	INTRODUCTION
116	It is well established that inadequate fluid intake adversely affects physical and
117	psychological performance on the short-term (i.e., acute dehydration), and may increase the risk
118	of chronic disease long-term (i.e., poor fluid intake behaviors). Thus, efforts to adequately assess
119	hydration status allow for a direct means of addressing changes in total body water. A plethora of
120	methods used to determine or capture changes in hydration status are succinctly summarized in
121	D
122	previous literature (1). While laboratory or field-based methods for hydration assessment in
123	research settings provide accurate measures of body water regulation and homeostasis, these
124	EP
125	measures are not feasible in the general population. Cheuvront and Sawka (2) proposed a
126	framework that includes morning body weight (W), first urine void color (U), and thirst
127	TE
128	perception (T; WUT framework) as a simple approach for laypersons to determine the adequacy
129	of their fluid intake. Individual changes in W (>1% body mass, kg), U (>5 A.U. using a 1 – 8-
130	point urine color chart (3)), and T (conscious desire to consume fluids) provide evidence of
131	inadequate fluid intake; however, a combination of changes that exceed these thresholds further
132	strengthens the likelihood of insufficient fluid intake.

134	C Despite its simplicity, rigorous science and compelling evidence support the WUT model
135	and the individual variables included in the model. Once body weight decreases by 1% of overall
136	A
137	body mass, confidence increases that total body water (TBW) decreased due to deficits in fluid
138	intake, rather than sensible and insensible fluid loss. Similarly, as TBW decreases, plasma
139	osmolality increases, triggering internal mechanisms responsible for the presence of thirst (4),
140	and renal water retention increases in response to increasing arginine vasopressin (AVP)
141	concentrations – thereby concentrating the urine. This increase in urine concentration can be
142	accurately matched to a urine color comparison chart and correlates with changes in urine
143	osmolality and urine specific gravity (3).

145	validity of using this framework has not been fully explored. Sekiguchi and colleagues (5)
146	recently tested the WUT framework and found that exceeding cut-point thresholds on two
147	D
148	components (W & U, and U & T) could accurately detect hypohydration, a state of body water

150	EP

152	ability of the WUT framework to detect hypohydration, respectively However, neither of these

156	that allows for the direct assessment of the efficacy of the proposed model. Importantly, this
157	previous work considered WUT components as binary predictors (i.e., value exceeds a threshold
158	or not), rather than treating each component as a continuous measure that can linearly or non-
159	C
160	linearly change with the likelihood of dehydration. Lastly, as evidenced in the work of Sekiguchi
161	C
162	et el., Keefe et al., and Wardenaar et al., the WUT framework assumes that each component
163	contributes equally to determining the likelihood of dehydration. Although this conjecture is
164	A
165	reasonable based on the originally proposed model, it is unlikely to be accurate, since the
166	sensitivity of each WUT component for predicting dehydration differs in reference to body water
167	regulation, suggesting unequal weighting is likely.

169	incredibly appealing due to its simplicity, ease and cost effectiveness. A properly weighted
170	predictive model provides individuals a better understanding as to which of these variables offers
171	an improved ability to determine their fluid needs. However, further development and validation
172	is required to rigorously test the model’s predictive accuracy across multiple scenarios. Thus, the
173	purpose of this study was two-fold: 1) to assess the utility of the WUT framework in predicting
174	D

176	component's independent and interactive importance in predicting dehydration. We hypothesize
177	EP
178	that changes in each WUT component (body mass loss, increased urine concentration, increased

180	TE
181	different across groups undergoing varying levels of body water manipulation. Further, we
182	hypothesize that changes in body mass would be the component of greatest importance when
183	determining the likelihood of dehydration. The results from this study have broad potential
184	applications in field-based settings for individuals who live, work, and train, in environments

INTRODUCTION
It is well established that inadequate fluid intake adversely affects physical and
psychological performance on the short-term (i.e., acute dehydration), and may increase the risk
of chronic disease long-term (i.e., poor fluid intake behaviors). Thus, efforts to adequately assess
hydration status allow for a direct means of addressing changes in total body water. A plethora of
methods used to determine or capture changes in hydration status are succinctly summarized in
D
previous literature (1). While laboratory or field-based methods for hydration assessment in
research settings provide accurate measures of body water regulation and homeostasis, these
EP
measures are not feasible in the general population. Cheuvront and Sawka (2) proposed a
framework that includes morning body weight (W), first urine void color (U), and thirst
TE

of their fluid intake. Individual changes in W (>1% body mass, kg), U (>5 A.U. using a 1 – 8-
point urine color chart (3)), and T (conscious desire to consume fluids) provide evidence of
inadequate fluid intake; however, a combination of changes that exceed these thresholds further
strengthens the likelihood of insufficient fluid intake.
C
C Despite its simplicity, rigorous science and compelling evidence support the WUT model
and the individual variables included in the model. Once body weight decreases by 1% of overall
A
body mass, confidence increases that total body water (TBW) decreased due to deficits in fluid
intake, rather than sensible and insensible fluid loss. Similarly, as TBW decreases, plasma
osmolality increases, triggering internal mechanisms responsible for the presence of thirst (4),
and renal water retention increases in response to increasing arginine vasopressin (AVP)
concentrations – thereby concentrating the urine. This increase in urine concentration can be
accurately matched to a urine color comparison chart and correlates with changes in urine
osmolality and urine specific gravity (3).
While the WUT framework is theoretically and scientifically sound, the utility and
validity of using this framework has not been fully explored. Sekiguchi and colleagues (5)
recently tested the WUT framework and found that exceeding cut-point thresholds on two
D
components (W & U, and U & T) could accurately detect hypohydration, a state of body water
deficit, as measured by urine specific gravity and urine osmolality. Work by Keefe et al. (6) and
EP
Wardenaar et al. (7) supported and contrasted the work of Sekiguchi et al. (5), and thus the
ability of the WUT framework to detect hypohydration, respectively However, neither of these
TE
studies tested the WUT framework’s ability to detect dehydration following a body water
manipulation protocol where body water is actively lost from the body (i.e., sweating), a design
that allows for the direct assessment of the efficacy of the proposed model. Importantly, this
previous work considered WUT components as binary predictors (i.e., value exceeds a threshold
or not), rather than treating each component as a continuous measure that can linearly or non-
C
linearly change with the likelihood of dehydration. Lastly, as evidenced in the work of Sekiguchi
C
et el., Keefe et al., and Wardenaar et al., the WUT framework assumes that each component
contributes equally to determining the likelihood of dehydration. Although this conjecture is
A
reasonable based on the originally proposed model, it is unlikely to be accurate, since the
sensitivity of each WUT component for predicting dehydration differs in reference to body water
regulation, suggesting unequal weighting is likely.
A properly weighted predictive model using WUT to assess hydration status en masse is
incredibly appealing due to its simplicity, ease and cost effectiveness. A properly weighted
predictive model provides individuals a better understanding as to which of these variables offers
an improved ability to determine their fluid needs. However, further development and validation
is required to rigorously test the model’s predictive accuracy across multiple scenarios. Thus, the
purpose of this study was two-fold: 1) to assess the utility of the WUT framework in predicting
D
dehydration following a body water manipulation protocol and 2) to determine each WUT
component's independent and interactive importance in predicting dehydration. We hypothesize
EP
that changes in each WUT component (body mass loss, increased urine concentration, increased
perception of thirst) and the probabilities of hypohydration therein would be significantly
TE
different across groups undergoing varying levels of body water manipulation. Further, we
hypothesize that changes in body mass would be the component of greatest importance when
determining the likelihood of dehydration. The results from this study have broad potential
applications in field-based settings for individuals who live, work, and train, in environments
likely to induce dehydration and can be used to drive improved hydration behaviors across free-
C
living populations.

METHODS
A
Study Design
This was approached in two phases; an initial observational design where daily hydration
measures were collected in free-living men and women, followed by a randomized design where
subjects were allocated into one of three groups that manipulated total body water. The initial
phase (Phase 1) of the study combined 24-h and first-morning free-living hydration variables
across two studies (Study 1 [n = 58], three consecutive days of 24-h free-living hydration
assessment; Study 2 [n = 35], seven consecutive days of 24-h free living hydration assessment)
to determine daily reference change values for changes in WUT components. The second phase
of the study (Phase 2, Study 2 only) consisted of a two-hour passive heating protocol (40℃, 50%
relative humidity) followed by randomization to one of three groups that manipulated total body
water over a 24-h period (see Measures section for fluid prescription procedures for each group).
The study design schematic is illustrated in Figure 1.

Participants
EP
Ninety-three participants (females, n = 47; see Table 1 for other participant
TE
demographics) between the ages of 18 – 35 y were recruited from a university in the
Southeastern and Northeastern United States. Prior to enrollment, participants completed a
general medical health history questionnaire to ensure they did not meet any of the following
exclusion criteria: 1) no chronic health problems or diseases that alter body water regulation or
one's ability to thermoregulate, 2) no history of exertional heat illness within the last three years
C
and no history of cardiovascular, metabolic or respiratory disease, 3) no previous surgery of the
C
gastrointestinal tract that could impact body water regulation, 4) no pharmacologic drug
treatment in the previous 15 days, 5) not exercising more than 10 hours per week, and 6) not
A
actively attempting to gain or lose bodyweight. For female participants, all testing visits occurred
during the early follicular phase (days 1-8) of the menstrual cycle to maintain consistency among
fluid regulatory hormones across female participants (8). Study 1 tested naturally cycling
females (no contraceptive use) only, whereas Study 2 did not control for contraceptive use.
However, for Study 2, females were excluded if the contraceptive they used reduced the number
of menstrual cycles they experienced throughout a 12-month period. All participants provided
written and informed consent prior to participation in this study, which was approved by the
Institutional Review Boards at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro (#18-0063) and
the University of Connecticut (H17-129). All study procedures conformed with the Declaration
of Helsinki.

percentage. Note that throughout this manuscript, SI units of mass (kg) are used to describe
TE
weight (W) since electronic scales measure weight as a function of the kilograms of force the

scheduled testing visit. Participants were instructed to use the 100 mL specimen container to

C
Experimental Trial. For Phase 1 of this study, a total of 419 d (observations) were included;
Study 1 included 174 d (58 participants x 3 consecutive days), and Study 2 included 245 d (35
A
participants x 7 consecutive days). The number of observations from Study 1 and Study 2

Participants were free to go about their normal daily activities and behaviors as the specific goal

EP
On day 7 (Phase 2, Study 2), following the return of the 24 h and first morning void urine
samples, a NBM, and rating of perceived thirst, participants entered an environmental chamber
TE
and remained in a seated position for two hours (40°C, 50% relative humidity) to induce passive
fluid loss. Participants wore shorts, t-shirt, socks, shoes, and their undergarments during this 2 h
seated and passive heat exposure. Another NBM measurement was taken at the conclusion of

On day 8, participants returned their 24 h urine sample and first morning void urine samples,

Measures
Anthropometric Measures. NBM was measured to the nearest 0.1 kg (Study 1, Defender R7000
Extreme, OHAUS Corporation, Parsippany, NJ; WB-800S Plus, Tanita Corporation, Tokyo,
Japan). Height was measured to the nearest 0.1cm using a wall-mounted stadiometer (Studies 1

Technologies, Santa Cruz, CA) on the right side of the body (9, 10); measures were taken at the
chest, abdomen, and thigh for males and suprailiac, triceps, and thigh for women. Body fat
percentage was calculated using the Siri equation (11).

EP
Perceived Thirst. Thirst was assessed daily using a 9-point Likert Scale with associated word
anchors of 1, "Not Thirsty at All"; 3, "A Little Thirsty"; 5, "Moderately Thirsty"; 7, "Very
TE
Thirsty"; and 9, "Very, Very Thirsty" (12).

measured for urine specific gravity (USG), urine osmolality (UOSMO) and urine color (UCOL). USG

C

C
Model 3320, Advanced Instruments, Norwood, MA). UCOL was rated on a 8-point widely used

(Table 2).
Day 8 Fluid Prescription. In Study 2, between day 7 and day 8, participants were randomized to
one of 3 different fluid intake conditions: Recommended Intake (Control), Moderate Fluid
Restriction (Sweat Loss), and Complete Fluid Restriction (Restriction). Participants in the
Control group were provided and told to consume the recommended amount of fluid intake for
