males), plus any estimated body water losses incurred from resting in the environmental chamber

(rounded to the nearest 500mL) before their arrival to the lab on day 8. The Sweat Loss group
was asked to consume only the estimated fluid lost through sweating in the environmental
EP
chamber. The Restriction group was asked not to consume any fluids, including any water-heavy

Step 3: Assessing the Variable Importance of Body Mass, Urine Color, and Thirst. Because the

TE
diagram. All statistical analyses were completed using R statistical program (code available upon

DISCUSSION
TE
The purpose of this study was to empirically test the WUT framework for the determination
of hydration status following a body water manipulation protocol and to evaluate and establish
the relative contribution of each independent and interactive component. We hypothesized that
the WUT would be an effective framework for predicting a change in hydration status, and that
C
change in nude body mass would be most important in determining hydration status. From these
C
analyses, we have reported empirically based reference change values for each component of the
WUT framework, demonstrated the effectiveness of these non-linear models in predicting
A
hydration status following a fluid manipulation trial, and presented an updated WUT model that
is scaled based on the independent and combined effects of body mass change, urine color, and
thirst. These results support and advance the use of the WUT in assessing hydration status with a
simple, easy, and cost-effective method. The reference change values (RCV) presented are based
on a large and diverse sample of young adults across more than 400 observations (i.e., days of
participant data collection), enabling a statistically sound number of observations for the day-to-
day variability and increasing the generalizability of these results.
Importantly, RCV equations calculated here are theoretically reasonable; for example, a ~1%
change in body mass was determined to be more likely or very likely dehydrated. Our findings
also show that the probability of dehydration was very likely (90%) in instances where body
D
mass changes exceeded 1.25% body mass loss, which is largely aligned with previously
published findings (16, 19). Specifically, Cheuvront et al. found that a body mass change of
EP
1.3% produced an 80% likelihood of dehydration based on a 5mmol/kg increase in plasma
osmolality (16). While the probability of dehydration was lower for similar body mass changes
TE
in Cheuvront et al. (16), the approximation of their findings to ours lends to the consistency
between samples and allows us to make an informed assumption that the participants in our
sample had an acute increase in plasma osmolality. Importantly, the differences in the probability
of dehydration between our sample and the calculations by Cheuvront et al. (16) is a result of the

lower (approximately 42% lower) day-to-day variability observed in the present study. However,
C
this is expected since the sample size used in the current analysis is more than 5 times larger than
C
Cheuvront et al. (16) thus reducing the impact of more extreme values on average intra-
individual variability. It must also be noted that it is commonly thought that the daily upper
A
range for variation in body mass to identify an individual as euhydrated is ± 1% body mass (1,
20, 21), however, based on our findings, this may lend to a more likely probability of
dehydration, likely reflecting the large inter-individual variability of fluid needs. Yet, this does
not change our recommendations from an application perspective: if the day-to-day variation in
body mass change exceeds 1% of normal body mass, attempts to consume additional fluids
throughout the day are warranted.
When examining the probability of dehydration based on urine color and thirst perception,
we found that an individual is very likely to be dehydrated with a change in urine color that is
equivalent to 2 levels on a previously validated scale(3), and a change in thirst of one unit using
a 9-point Likert scale. Our findings are consistent with previous literature that show the
D
relationships between dehydration and changes in urinary (13, 22–24) and thirst indices (12, 19,
25). Determining the influence of dehydration on urine color using receiver operator
EP
characteristic analyses, McKenzie et al. (13) found that a urine color of 5 A.U. corresponded to a
level of dehydration that approximated 2% body mass loss. Cheuvront et al., (16) also observed
TE
that a urine color of 6.5 A.U. paralleled 2.5% body mass loss, further supporting the association
between dehydration and changes in urine color. Our findings are complementary, in that, a 2
A.U. increase in urine color exhibited a 90% probability of dehydration, and thus could be used
independently or in combination with the work by McKenzie and colleagues to assist in guiding
fluid intake. For example, following a dehydration protocol, a change in an individual’s urine
C
color may change from 3 A.U. (before dehydration protocol) to 5 A.U. (following the
C
dehydration protocol). In this example, the change of 2 A.U. would indicate a 90% probability of
dehydration, and by using the findings from McKenzie, et al. (13), may also indicate that the
A
overall magnitude of dehydration would be approximately 2% of body mass loss. While this
example is theoretical in nature, it must be acknowledged that by using the results of our findings
(i.e., a 2 A.U. change in urine color corresponding to a 90% probability of dehydration) as a
standalone may not provide an individual with an indication of how much fluid to consume. We
must also consider the findings of previous literature that suggests dietary behaviors may alter
urine color, thus potentially decreasing the efficacy of this measure as a tool to monitor hydration
status (26, 27). Thus, if urine color is to be used as a determination of adequacy of fluid intake, it
may be prudent to consider adding in an additional metric such as body mass to be used in
combination to determine fluid needs.
Previous work (12, 19, 25, 28, 29) exploring the effect of dehydration on thirst perception
D
has consistently shown that greater levels of dehydration elicit a greater thirst response.
However, this previous work did not objectively quantify the likelihood of dehydration based on
EP
changes in thirst perception. Our findings add to the existing literature by providing nuanced
insights on how changes in first morning thirst can be used to aid in determining the adequacy of
TE
fluid intake. Interestingly, we observed that a 1 A.U. change in thirst perception resulted in a
90% probability of dehydration. While this low threshold for increased probability of
dehydration with a small change in perceived thirst could be due to the sensitivity of the measure
(the Thirst scale used in this study was an ordinal scale that increased by increments of 1 A.U.),
the contributions of both volumetric and osmotic factors contributing to the thirst response
C
cannot be neglected (30). We want to highlight that our assessment of first morning perception of
C
thirst is essential as previous literature (28, 29) shows that ingestion of fluids minimizes
perceived thirst despite sustained levels of dehydration.
A Cheuvront and Sawka (2) proposed the WUT framework for lay use in healthy, active,
and low-risk populations as a daily method of determining fluid intake adequacy. While the
inception of the framework lacked the prospective validation work to determine its efficacy, the
scientific principles guiding its development and use are well established (3, 16, 25, 31). In the
current study, we implemented a randomized water manipulation protocol to elicit either
dehydration or euhydration. Unlike the original WUT framework by Cheuvront and Sawka (2)
and the recent validation of the framework by Sekiguchi et al. (5), we scaled the associated Venn
diagram based on the data-driven importance of each component. Changes in body mass (relative
importance, 58%), was found to be the most important component to use to determine the
adequacy of fluid intake, followed by thirst (relative importance, 26%), and then urine color
D
(relative importance, 3%). We also found significant interactions between body mass change and
urine color, body mass change and thirst in predicting dehydration, but not between thirst and
EP
urine color. Given the differences in weighting of each individual component, as well as the two-
way and three-way interactions of each component, the determination of likely and very likely
TE
probably of dehydration proposed in the original model is not equally weighted and a greater
emphasis should be placed on day-to-day body mass changes and presence of thirst.
Strengths and Limitations
This study applied rigorous statistical analyses to extensive daily body mass, urinary, and
C
thirst observations from a diverse sample and demonstrated good validity of the WUT against a
C
fluid intake manipulation and allowed us to develop sound reference change values (Step 1 of the
analysis) for each component of the WUT framework to use for the subsequent analyses and
A
comparisons. Lastly, the utilization of a randomized process to test the water intake experimental
trials adds to the confidence in our findings.
However, there are study limitations that should be noted. First, the data from Study 2
required participants to fully adhere to the fluid restriction protocol. If individuals did not adhere
to the protocol, we may expect some of the collected variables (e.g., urine osmolality) to reflect
this deviation from instructions – providing a reasonable justification for exclusion from
analysis. However, because of the correlation between our three WUT variables, any exclusion
based on urinary criteria that indicated a lack of strict adherence to the protocol would introduce
bias into our results and assume that individual variability in response to these protocols has an
upper limit; a claim for which we currently have no basis for making. We, therefore, chose not to
D
exclude any participants from the analysis, yet we could still demonstrate the practicality of the
WUT model in most cases. Based on the data presented here, future studies should consider the
EP
reasonableness of their data in response to fluid manipulation.
TE
Secondly, and as already alluded, these results should be generalized only to a similar sample
of healthy young adults and may not apply to other populations, including those with medical or
other thermoregulatory concerns, or those individuals that are regularly exposed to dehydrating
activities (e.g., athletes, laborers, soldiers) (32, 33). For example, the RCV models or variable
importance values presented here may not apply to older persons, as the thirst mechanism
C
becomes less sensitive with aging (34). The "normal" observed variability in each of these
C
variables may therefore be different (i.e., greater) in other populations, and thus these RCV
equations should be recomputed for specific samples of interest. However, the within-person
A
variation in WUT variables is relatively stable, even in disease states, and thus researchers and
practitioners should tentatively proceed with applying these results to a wider array of
populations. Lastly, the ridge regression and resultant Venn diagram utilized all available data
(due to sample size for the fluid manipulation protocol, we did not use training, test, and
validation splits) and thus could be overfitting to our specific sample. Caution is therefore
advised when attempting to apply the relative importance of each WUT component. Although
we are confident in the relative ranking of the individual and combined effects of the WUT
framework within this study population, the exact contribution to the probability of dehydration
is less certain in other populations (e.g., older adults, children, certain illnesses eliciting emesis
or diarrhea, etc.). Future investigations could confirm the veracity of these model coefficients
and variable importance values.
CONCLUSIONS
D
EP
Changes in first morning body mass, urine color, and thirst can be used independently,
and in combination to determine the adequacy of fluid intake on a day-to-day basis. When using
TE
the WUT framework, an approach that can be feasibly performed among a lay population, day-
to-day changes in body mass hold the largest weight in determining the likelihood of
dehydration, followed by changes in thirst perception, and then urine color. It is necessary to
continue exploring the utility of the WUT framework across varying populations such as an
ageing and/or diseased population to derive a more comprehensive and valid use case.

Utility of VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT
Baseline Evaluations for Acute Concussion
Identification in Collegiate Athletes
Findings From the NCAA-DoD Concussion Assessment,
Research and Education (CARE) Consortium
Lyndsey M. Ferris,* PhD, OD, Anthony P. Kontos,y PhD, Shawn R. Eagle,y PhD, ATC ,

Background: The Vestibular/Ocular-Motor Screening (VOMS) is a valuable component of acute (\72 hours) sports-related con-
cussion (SRC) assessments and is increasingly used with the Immediate Post-concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing
(ImPACT) instrument and the third edition of the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT3). Research has suggested that
VOMS acute postinjury scores are useful in identifying acute concussion. However, the utility of preseason baseline measure-
ments to improve diagnostic accuracy remains ambiguous. To this end, there is a need to determine how reliable VOMS baseline
assessments are across years and whether incorporating individuals’ baseline performance improves diagnostic yield for acute
concussions.
Purpose: To analyze VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT to evaluate the test-retest reliability of consecutive-year preseason baseline
assessments to directly compare the diagnostic utility of these tools when incorporating baseline assessments versus using post-
injury data alone to identify acute SRC.
Study Design: Cohort study (diagnosis); Level of evidence, 2.
Methods: Preseason and postinjury VOMS, SCAT3, ImPACT Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS), and ImPACT composite
scores were analyzed for 3958 preseason (47.7% female) and 496 acute (48 hours) SRC (37.5% female) collegiate athlete eval-
uations in the National Collegiate Athletic Association—Department of Defense Concussion Assessment Research and Education
Consortium. Descriptive statistics, Kolmogorov-Smirnov significance, and Cohen d effect size were calculated. Consecutive-year
baseline reliability was evaluated for a subset of 447 athlete encounters using Pearson r, Cohen k, Cohen d, and 2-way mixed
intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Wilcoxon signed rank tests were used to determine the statistical significance between
population performances, and the 90% reliable change index (RCI) was calculated from the test-retest results. Preseason to post-
injury change scores were then calculated from each tool’s RCI. Finally, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses
were conducted, and DeLong method was used to compare the area under the curve (AUC) of raw postinjury scores versus
change scores from preseason baseline assessments. Potential effects of sex, medical history (learning disorders or attention-
deficit/hyperactivity disorder), and outlier data were also explored.
Results: Effect sizes were large, and overall predictive utilities were clinically useful for postinjury VOMS Total (d = 2.44; AUC =
0.85), the SCAT3 Symptom Evaluation total severity score (d = 1.74; AUC = 0.82), and the ImPACT PCSS total severity score (d =
1.67; AUC = 0.80). Comparatively, effect sizes were small and predictive utilities were poor for Standardized Assessment of Con-
cussion (SAC), modified Balance Error Scoring System (mBESS), and all ImPACT composites (d = 0.11-0.46; AUC = 0.48-0.59).
Preseason baseline test-retest reliability was poor to moderate (r = 0.23-0.52; k = 0.32-0.36; ICC = 0.36-0.68) for all assessments

Evaluation, SAC, mBESS), ImPACT PCSS, or ImPACT composites did not significantly improve AUCs.
Conclusion: VOMS Total and symptom severity (SCAT3, PCSS) total scores had large effect sizes and clinically useful AUCs for
identifying acute concussion. However, all tools demonstrated high within-patient test-retest variability, resulting in poor reliability.
The findings in this sample of collegiate athletes suggest that incorporating baseline assessments does not significantly increase
diagnostic yield for acute concussion.
